# One North America: full text

The English text of onenorthamerica.org, generated from the pages on 2026-11-06. Spanish: https://onenorthamerica.org/es/llms-full.txt

Source: https://onenorthamerica.org/

A proposal for the future of the continent

# Three countries. ~~Three tariffs.~~ One market.

A customs union for North America: one tariff at the edge, goods moving freely inside. Everything else stays national.

- 521 million people

- ≈$33 trillion economy

- ≈30% of world output

One North America puts one tariff at its edge, lets goods cross without certificates of origin and draws factories from Asia, keeping a young continent of 521 million people the world’s most productive region, strong enough to take on China, India and the EU.

Each icon opens its part of the case.

01 · The union at a glance

## Five changes. Everything else stays national.

A customs union is the step after a free trade area. It changes how goods are treated at the border, and nothing else.

### One common tariff

Every imported product pays the same duty, whether it lands in Vancouver, Houston or Manzanillo.

### Free circulation

Once inside North America, goods cross between the three countries with no customs clearance and no certificates of origin.

### Shared trade rules

One policy on antidumping, safeguards and competition, applied by each country’s own agencies under mirror laws. No new supranational bureaucracy.

### Shared revenue

Tariff revenue is split by formula: part to the country where goods arrive, the rest according to each country’s contribution to regional trade.

### One trade policy

One policy toward the rest of the world, backed by the buying power of 521 million people: imports cost less, and the region competes with China, India and the European Union as one.

### Stays national

- Currency

- Immigration and citizenship

- Taxes and budgets

- Laws and courts

- Elections and government

- Defense and foreign policy

Labor mobility is not part of a customs union. It is best handled separately, through a managed agreement among neighbors (see “Neighbors already” below).

02 · The common tariff

## One tariff book for the whole continent.

Today each country charges its own duties on goods from outside the region. In the union there would be one schedule. Here is how sample products compare today, and where the common rate would land.

The clearest case

### One car. Three tariffs.

In 2024 the United States and Canada both put a 100% tariff on Chinese electric cars. In January 2026 Canada agreed to let in up to 49,000 a year at 6.1%, while Mexico set its own rate at 50%.

When neighbors charge different rates, only rules of origin and border checks keep the cheapest door from becoming everyone’s door. A common tariff closes it by design.

#### Tariff on a Chinese-made electric car, 2026

Percent of the car’s value

In a customs union: one rate, whichever port the car enters. No cheapest door.

U.S.: 2.5% MFN plus 100% Section 301 duty (2024), excluding other duties added since 2025. Canada: 6.1% MFN plus 100% surtax (Oct. 2024); since Jan. 2026, up to 49,000 vehicles a year at 6.1%. Mexico: 50% under the 2026 reform. Sources: USTR, Government of Canada, DOF; press coverage (CNBC, Reuters).

### The tariff book, line by line

Duty on imports from outside the region, percent of value

Rates are those applied to countries without a trade agreement (MFN), excluding temporary additional duties imposed since 2025. Mexico’s rates reflect the reform in force since January 1, 2026. Common rates are illustrative. Sources: U.S. Harmonized Tariff Schedule, Canada Customs Tariff, Mexico’s LIGIE (DOF, Dec. 29, 2025), WTO Tariff & Trade Data.

### Already the same: lock it in

In 2023, 2,278 tariff lines (40.6%) already carried the same lowest rate in Mexico and the United States, covering 61% of U.S. imports and 66% of Mexico’s. These go first. The region has done this before: under NAFTA, the three countries aligned their outside tariffs on computers and color TV tubes.

40.6% of tariff lines already identical (U.S.–Mexico, 2023)

### Different: converge to the lowest

Where rates differ, converge on the lowest rate consistent with WTO commitments, as a 2005 trinational task force recommended. The union must be more open on the whole than what it replaces, as GATT Article XXIV requires.

### Where buying power counts: calibrate

North America imports about $500 billion a year in machinery and equipment and $400 billion in vehicles, 30% to 50% of what its suppliers export. When a buyer is that large, a jointly set tariff can lower the prices the region pays.

### Farm goods: pool the quotas

Sensitive products such as dairy and sugar would face one duty, and their import quotas would be pooled and auctioned among importers across the whole region.

03 · One perimeter

## Pay once at the edge. Move freely inside.

Follow one part: imported from Asia, assembled in Monterrey, sold in Detroit.

**Customs stops**

2 1

**Certificates of origin**

1 0

**Agency fees at the border**

1–3% 0

### Enters North America

Pays Mexico’s duty, which may differ from the U.S. or Canadian rate for the very same item.

Pays the common North American duty once, the same at any port.

### Assembled in Monterrey

The factory traces every input’s origin to prove enough regional content.

The factory buys inputs wherever they are best. No origin arithmetic.

### Crosses at Laredo

Origin certificate, customs agency fees of 1–3%, unloading and reloading between warehouses. If it falls short of the rule, it pays the U.S. tariff.

Circulates as a North American good. No origin certification, no customs clearance for goods.

### Sold in Detroit

Every cost along the way is in the final price.

Lower costs, faster delivery, one continental market.

Agency fees run 1–3% of invoice value: what a customs agency at the U.S.–Mexico border typically charges, before warehousing, reloading and waiting time.

Why it matters now

### A free trade area runs on paperwork, and the paperwork keeps growing.

### How much of a car must be North American to cross duty-free

Regional value content required for passenger vehicles

U.S.–Canada FTA (1989): 50%. NAFTA: 62.5% once fully phased in. USMCA: 66% (2020), 69%, 72%, 75% (2023), plus labor-value and steel rules. Sources: USMCA Ch. 4; Congressional Research Service. In a customs union, internal trade needs no origin rule.

### The 2025 stress test

Share of U.S. imports entering duty-free under USMCA, before and after the 2025 tariffs

When tariffs hit partners in 2025, firms rushed to certify origin. It worked, and showed the cost: every shipment must prove it is North American. In a customs union, it simply is.

Dallas Fed (2026): about 50% (Mexico) and under 40% (Canada) before, about 80% by July 2025. USTR (2026): 94.7% of vehicle imports from Canada and Mexico claimed USMCA in 2025.

04 · Built in North America

## Thirty years of building a region.

The three countries no longer just buy and sell from each other: they produce together. Three decades of evidence, brought up to date.

### Mexico’s non-oil exports

Billions of U.S. dollars per day

1993, 2013: Serra Puche (2015), INEGI. 2025: INEGI, $643.6 billion of non-oil exports. Oil is now 3% of Mexico’s exports.

### Foreign direct investment in Mexico

Billions of U.S. dollars per year

Averages: Serra Puche (2015), INEGI. 2025: Secretaría de Economía, $40,871 million, the highest on record.

### Mexico’s openness to trade

Exports plus imports, percent of GDP

Before and after joining GATT (1986): Serra Puche (2015). 2024: World Bank data.

### The great rerouting: where U.S. imports come from

U.S. goods imports, billions of dollars, 2017 and 2024

In 2023 Mexico overtook China as the largest source of U.S. imports for the first time in two decades. Sources: Bureau of Labor Statistics (2017), U.S. Census Bureau (2024).

The 2025 paradox

### Tariffs on everyone. Mexico came out ahead.

In 2025 Washington raised tariffs on almost every supplier. But goods that proved they were North American still crossed duty-free, and most of Mexico’s did.

An accidental perimeter, drawn by one country and open only with paperwork. A common tariff would draw it on purpose: set by all three, built to last.

#### Effective U.S. tariff by supplier, July 2025

Duties collected, percent of the value of imports

Brazil and India, not shown: 50% announced rates from August 2025. Sources: Federal Reserve Bank of New York (2025); CRS (2026); Cleary Gottlieb (2025).

### Each country doing what it does best

Mexico

#### Factory of the continent

Attract production of intermediate and manufactured goods now made in Southeast Asia, using a young workforce close to the world’s largest consumer market.

United States

#### Advanced manufacturing

Make the capital-intensive industrial goods the region now buys from Europe and Northeast Asia.

Canada

#### Energy and resources

Supply the energy, minerals and materials a growing continental industry demands.

The scrambled egg theorem

## You can’t unscramble an egg. You can only move forward.

Thirty years of free trade have turned three economies into one production system. Pulling it apart would break all three; standing still keeps every cost of the border. Scroll to see why only one move is left.

1993

### Three eggs.

Before NAFTA, three economies sat side by side, each behind its own tariff wall. They traded with each other, but production stayed mostly national.

$293B U.S. goods trade with Canada and Mexico in 1993.

1994–2024

### Scrambled.

Free trade cracked the shells. Factories spread their work across all three countries: some car parts cross the border seven or eight times before they reach a finished vehicle, and each dollar Mexico exports to the United States carries about 40 cents of U.S. content.

$1.6T U.S. goods trade with Canada and Mexico in 2024, 5.5 times as much.

2017 · 2025

### Try to unscramble it.

It has been tried. In 2017 the United States threatened to leave NAFTA; it ended up signing the USMCA. In 2025 tariffs hit both neighbors; instead of leaving, firms certified their goods as North American.

≈80% of U.S. imports from Canada and Mexico claimed USMCA by July 2025, up from under half.

Next

### Forward: one perimeter.

If the egg can’t be unscrambled, the rational move is to finish the dish: one common tariff around what is already one economy. Inside, no one asks where an ingredient came from.

0 certificates of origin inside the union.

Theorem

Once economies have produced together for a generation, they cannot be pulled apart without breaking all of them.

Corollary

A free trade area cannot stand still either: its rules of origin keep tightening and its costs keep rising. The only stable move is forward, to a customs union.

The scrambled egg theorem: Jaime Serra Puche. Goods trade: U.S. Census Bureau (1993, 2024). Parts crossing borders: Congressional Research Service, IF11387 (2021). U.S. content: Koopman, Wang & Wei (2014). NAFTA renegotiation: Congressional Research Service (2026). USMCA claims: Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas (2026).

05 · The demographic advantage

## A continent that stays young.

Around 2014–15, North America’s workforce began to outgrow China’s. China’s working-age population peaked in 2014 and is now shrinking; North America’s keeps growing to 2050.

### People of working age (15–64)

### Dependents per working-age person

Under 15 and over 64, per person aged 15–64 · 2025 → 2050

Source: UN WPP 2024, our calculations. The same complementarity appears in 2012 data in Serra Puche (2015).

Median age, 2025

The next step is to put this combined pyramid to work through a trilateral circular-mobility agreement that matches labor supply and demand across the year, backed by security cooperation.

06 · Neighbors already

## Shared faith, shared languages, shared families.

Integration works best between people who already have much in common. North Americans do.

official languages in Canada, English and French, link it to both its neighbors and to the wider world.

Mobility, managed and among neighbors

### Work where you are needed. Come home.

A trilateral circular-mobility agreement would let workers move for a season or a project and return home, matching labor supply and demand across the year. To keep out illegal flows of labor from outside the region, it would be backed by security agreements, such as dismantling fentanyl supply networks in northwestern Mexico and fighting human trafficking in southern Mexico.

Europe shows why proximity matters. Over the past decade, immigration has become one of the most polarizing questions in European politics, with debates centered on integration across differences of language, religion and custom.

North America would start from common ground. Research finds that shared language and culture make migration both more likely and smoother for the people involved.

Adserà & Pytliková (2015); Belot & Ederveen (2012)

07 · Competing in the world

## The largest economy on Earth, competing as one.

With one trade policy, the region can compete with single countries such as China and India and with blocs such as the European Union, and stay the most productive region in the world.

Population, median age and workers (ages 15–64): UN World Population Prospects 2024, our calculations. Economy: nominal GDP in current U.S. dollars, approximate, from IMF and national accounts.

08 · How we get there

## Five stages. No leaps.

Negotiators become implementers: instead of trading concessions, the three countries build one trade policy step by step, so firms can adapt and no supranational institutions are needed.

### A new tariff book

Start with the tariff lines already equal in all three countries.

### Same standards

Align non-tariff barriers on every line in the new book.

### Complete the tariff

Add the common rate for all remaining lines.

### Competition policy

Harmonize national competition laws and institutions.

### Trade remedies

Harmonize antidumping, countervailing duties and safeguards.

- 1965 U.S.–Canada Auto Pact

- 1994 NAFTA: a free trade area

- 2015 NAFTA at 20: is a customs union next?

- 2020 USMCA

- 2025 Common-tariff proposal

- 2026 Joint review; annual reviews begin

- 2027 → The window for a customs union

09 · Questions

## Straight answers.

**What is a North American customs union?**

An agreement under which Canada, the United States and Mexico would charge one common tariff on imports from the rest of the world and let goods move freely among themselves, with no certificates of origin. Currency, immigration and government stay national.

**How is it different from the USMCA?**

The USMCA is a free trade area: goods cross duty-free only if they prove they are North American, and each country keeps its own tariffs toward the rest of the world. A customs union adds one common outside tariff, so origin no longer has to be proven inside.

**What is the scrambled egg theorem?**

The idea that after thirty years of free trade the three economies produce together so closely that they cannot be pulled apart without breaking all three, like a scrambled egg. The only rational move is forward, to a customs union.

**Is this a “North American Union” like the European Union?**

No. There is no common currency, no free movement of people and no supranational government. It is a customs union: one outer tariff, free circulation of goods, and coordinated trade rules applied by each country’s own institutions.

**Who sets the common tariff?**

The three governments, jointly, in stages. They start with the thousands of lines where rates already match and converge on the rest over a transition period. Each country keeps its seat and its voice.

**Would prices go up?**

The design points the other way. The common tariff converges toward the lowest rates and must be more open on the whole than today, as WTO rules require. Removing origin paperwork and border agency fees of 1–3% lowers costs further.

**What about China?**

Today, goods can enter through whichever partner charges less. With one common tariff every door charges the same, so the back door closes by design, and the region sets one coherent policy toward third countries instead of three.

**Who gets the tariff revenue?**

A two-part formula: a percentage to the country where goods arrive, and the remainder according to each country’s contribution to regional trade. The EU and the Southern African Customs Union already share revenue under their own formulas.

**What about immigration?**

Immigration stays national. Any labor mobility would come through a separate, managed circular-mobility agreement among the three neighbors, backed by security cooperation against illegal flows.

**What would it ask of Mexico?**

Reforms that strengthen the rule of law, competition and independent institutions, and a gradual end to the special regime for exporters so that their suppliers are local. The union is an anchor for that agenda, not a substitute for it.

**Didn’t the 2025 tariffs hurt Mexico?**

Less than almost anyone. Goods that qualified under the USMCA stayed duty-free, so in July 2025 imports from Mexico paid an effective 4.7%, against 40.4% for China. But that edge hangs on paperwork and on Washington alone; a customs union would make it permanent and shared.

**Is it realistic?**

It is ambitious, which is why it is staged. Since July 2026 the USMCA is reviewed every year; each review is a chance to set a destination instead of patching the agreement.

## An idea with deep foundations.

This vision rests on a published proposal for a North American common tariff and on decades of research into customs unions, rules of origin and North American integration.

- 2005 Council on Foreign Relations Building a North American Community

- 1997 Krueger Free Trade Agreements versus Customs Unions

- 1950 Viner The Customs Union Issue

01 · The argument

## From a free trade area to a customs union, in six steps.

Each step rests on evidence further down this page. Follow the chain, or jump to the step you doubt.

### The region already produces as one.

Some car parts cross the border seven or eight times, and each dollar Mexico exports to the United States carries about 40 cents of U.S. content. Thirty years of free trade cannot be unscrambled.

Evidence E1 E2 On the vision page

### A free trade area polices that integration at every border.

To cross duty-free, goods must prove they are North American. Customs agencies charge 1–3% of invoice value, and the content rule for cars has climbed from 50% to 75%.

Evidence E3 On the vision page

### Three outside tariffs drift apart.

In 2026 the same Chinese electric car pays 102.5% in the United States, 50% in Mexico and 6.1% within Canada’s quota. Rules of origin have to police every gap.

Evidence E4 On the vision page

### A customs union removes the border inside.

With one outside tariff, origin no longer matters within the region: no certificates, no customs for goods. Theory and trade law agree it can leave members and outsiders better off.

Evidence E5 On the vision page

### One tariff, set jointly, puts the region’s buying power to work.

North America buys 30–50% of what its machinery and vehicle suppliers export. A buyer that large can lower the prices it pays.

Evidence E6 On the vision page

### It can be built in stages, on a growing workforce.

National agencies under mirror laws, five stages and no new bureaucracy, in a region whose workforce grows while China’s and Europe’s shrink. Mexico’s own reforms remain the condition.

Evidence E7 E8 E9 E10 On the vision page

### Therefore: a common tariff as the anchor of a customs union.

Read the proposal

02 · The proposal

## A common tariff as the anchor for a customs union.

In March 2025, Pedro Noyola and Jaime Serra published “A Case for a North American Common Tariff” with the Wilson Center’s Mexico Institute. They review three decades of integration, explain why the move from NAFTA to the USMCA missed a chance to improve the model, and propose turning the free trade area into a customs union. In their own words:

“We propose that North America adopt a common tariff as an anchor for the natural evolution of the free trade area to a customs union.”

“The rules of origin threaten to become a protectionist vortex, a permanent source of trade diversion and net social loss.”

“A common tariff would eliminate origin certification and customs operations for intraregional trade.”

“A customs union with a common tariff would contribute more effectively than the USMCA to help keep North America as the most productive region of the world.”

[Read the paper at the Wilson Center](https://www.wilsoncenter.org/article/case-north-american-common-tariff)

### Jaime Serra Puche

Economist (PhD, Yale University). As Mexico’s Secretary of Commerce and Industrial Development (1988–1994) he led Mexico’s negotiation of NAFTA, and later served as Secretary of Finance. He is the founder and chairman of SAI Law & Economics.

### Pedro Noyola

Economist. He has worked with Jaime Serra on regional trade since the 1990s, including the 1997 report on regional trade agreements cited in the proposal, and is co-author of Modernidad y economía (1999).

03 · A lineage of ideas

## Seventy-five years in the making.

A North American customs union is not a new idea. It builds on the founding theory of customs unions and on a series of proposals from all three countries.

Introduces the test still used to grade trade agreements: do they create trade, or divert it from more efficient outside suppliers?

Describes integration as a ladder: free trade area, customs union, common market, economic union.

The region chooses a free trade area. Mexico still had high and dispersed tariffs, so a common tariff would have disrupted its production chains.

Reflections on Regionalism (Carnegie Endowment) sets three rules for agreements that create trade: respect GATT Article XXIV, treat outside investment without discrimination, and keep effective dispute settlement.

Toward a North American Community argues for deepening NAFTA, drawing lessons from Europe’s integration.

The C.D. Howe Institute’s framework for shaping a shared North American economic space.

Co-chaired by John Manley, Pedro Aspe and William Weld: a community whose boundaries “would be defined by a common external tariff and an outer security perimeter,” with the tariff negotiated sector by sector at the lowest rate consistent with multilateral obligations.

El TLC y la formación de una región (FCE) documents how two decades of NAFTA built a region that produces together, and closes by asking whether the next step is a customs union.

A common tariff as the anchor for a customs union, with a staged plan, a revenue formula and institutions that avoid supranational bodies.

04 · The evidence

## Every claim, and what supports it.

Ten claims, in the order of the argument. Each source is marked by kind, so you can see what rests on theory, on studies, on official data or on policy.

- Theory models and principles

- Study empirical research

- Data official statistics

- Policy laws, treaties, official reports

- Proposal the 2025 paper and earlier plans

E1

### The region already produces together

North American trade is not just exchange between separate economies but production shared across borders.

40¢ of U.S. content in each dollar Mexico exports to the United States

- Koopman, Wang & Wei (2014) Study Value-added accounting shows how much of each export contains inputs from partners: 40 cents of U.S. content per dollar of Mexican exports to the U.S. (2012).

- Noyola & Serra (2025) Proposal Industrial production in Mexico and the U.S. became statistically cointegrated after 1994, as did inflation and interest rates.

- U.S. Census Bureau Data Mexico and Canada are the two largest U.S. trading partners (2024).

- Serra Puche (2015) Study NAFTA turned Mexico into an export platform: non-oil exports grew from $0.12 billion a day in 1993 to $0.92 billion in 2013. Updated here: $1.76 billion a day in 2025 (INEGI).

E2

### Integration that can’t be undone

After a generation of free trade, the three economies produce together so closely that separating them would cost more than integrating further.

7–8× border crossings for some car parts before final assembly

- Jaime Serra Puche Theory The scrambled egg theorem: once the three economies have lived under NAFTA’s free trade, the eggs cannot be unscrambled; the key is to push forward, toward a customs union.

- Congressional Research Service (2021) Policy Some auto parts cross the border seven or eight times as they are assembled into larger products; some vehicle seats use components from four U.S. states and four Mexican locations.

- U.S. Census Bureau Data U.S. goods trade with Canada and Mexico grew from $293 billion in 1993 to $1.6 trillion in 2024.

- Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas (2026) Study When the 2025 tariffs hit, firms certified origin rather than leave: the share of U.S. imports claiming USMCA rose to about 80%.

- Federal Reserve Bank of New York (2025) Study In July 2025 imports from Mexico paid an effective U.S. tariff of 4.7% and those from Canada 3.0%, against 40.4% for China and 9.7% for all suppliers. Three in four of Mexico’s goods entered under USMCA, up from half in 2024.

- Congressional Research Service (2026) Policy Mexico was the largest supplier of U.S. goods imports in 2025, at $534.8 billion. The 10% global tariff that replaced the emergency tariffs in February 2026 exempted goods that meet USMCA rules of origin.

E3

### Rules of origin are costly and protectionist

Proving origin costs firms money, and origin thresholds tend to rise over time, diverting trade.

50% → 75% regional content a car needs to cross duty-free, 1989 to 2023

- Krueger (1993) Theory Free trade agreements as protectionist devices: rules of origin can extend protection across member markets.

- Anson, Cadot, Estevadeordal et al. (2005) Study Estimate the compliance costs of NAFTA’s rules of origin.

- Carrère & de Melo (2006) Study Show that different types of NAFTA origin rules carry different costs.

- Noyola & Serra (2025) Proposal The USMCA auto rule is about 20% more restrictive than NAFTA’s; a Mexican customs agency at the U.S. border costs 1–3% of invoice value.

- Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas (2026) Study When the 2025 tariffs exempted USMCA-compliant goods, the share of U.S. imports claiming the agreement rose from about 50% (Mexico) and under 40% (Canada) to about 80%: compliance is possible, and costly.

- USTR (2026) Policy 94.7% of vehicle imports from Canada and Mexico claimed USMCA treatment in 2025; the regional content rule for cars reached 75% in 2023.

E4

### Three tariffs drift apart

Without a common tariff, each country sets its own policy toward the same outside supplier, and origin rules must police the gaps.

3 different tariffs on the same Chinese electric car in 2026: 102.5%, 50% and 6.1%

- USTR (2024) Policy The Section 301 four-year review raised the U.S. tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 100%.

- Government of Canada (2024, 2026) Policy A 100% surtax on Chinese-made electric vehicles from October 2024; in January 2026, a quota of 49,000 vehicles a year at 6.1%.

- Government of Mexico (2025) Policy Tariffs of up to 50% on vehicles and other goods from countries without a trade agreement with Mexico, in force from 2026.

E5

### A customs union beats a free trade area

A customs union removes the need for rules of origin and, if its common tariff is set well, can benefit its members without hurting the rest of the world.

0 certificates of origin needed for trade inside a customs union

- Viner (1950) Theory Trade creation versus trade diversion: the standard for judging any regional agreement.

- Kemp & Wan (1976) Theory A customs union can always choose a common external tariff that leaves no member and no outsider worse off.

- Krueger (1997) Theory On welfare grounds, a customs union is always superior to a free trade area; free trade areas also build more resistance to further liberalization.

- GATT Article XXIV Policy Permits customs unions that cover substantially all trade and do not, on the whole, raise barriers to outsiders.

E6

### A large buyer can lower the prices it pays

When a region’s demand moves world prices, a calibrated tariff can lower import prices and raise its welfare.

30–50% of their suppliers’ exports: North America’s purchases of machinery and vehicles

- Optimal-tariff theory Theory Developed since Edgeworth in the late 19th century: the welfare-maximizing tariff is positive only for buyers with market power.

- Broda, Limão & Weinstein (2008) Study Countries do set higher tariffs on goods where they have more market power.

- Noyola & Serra (2025) Proposal North American imports of machinery and equipment (about $500 billion a year) and vehicles ($400 billion) equal 30–50% of suppliers’ exports.

E7

### Institutions without supranationalism

A customs union can run on coordinated national institutions rather than a new bureaucracy.

5 stages, each run by existing national agencies under mirror laws

- Noyola & Serra (2025) Proposal Mirror legal systems for trade remedies and competition policy, anchored in coordination provisions the USMCA already contains; Mexico would separate dumping calculations from injury findings, as Canada (CBSA and CITT) and the U.S. already do.

- Revenue-sharing precedents Policy The EU assigns part of customs revenue to the country of arrival; the Southern African Customs Union shares a common pool by a negotiated formula.

- CFR (2005) Proposal The trinational task force proposed a common external tariff without a supranational government or a common currency.

E8

### Demography favors North America

Combined, the three populations keep a growing workforce while rival economies shrink.

+5.3% North America’s working-age population, 2025–2050; China −25.3%, EU −17.0%

- UN World Population Prospects 2024 Data Working-age population 2025–2050: North America +5.3%, EU −17.0%, China −25.3%, Japan −25.6% (our calculations).

- Serra Puche (2015) Study Projected that North America’s workforce would begin to outgrow China’s around 2014–15. UN data now show China’s working-age population peaked in 2014.

- Noyola & Serra (2025) Proposal Propose a trilateral circular-mobility agreement to use the region’s combined demographic pyramid.

E9

### Shared culture eases mobility

People move more, and integrate more easily, where language and culture are shared.

43M people in the United States speak Spanish at home

- Adserà & Pytliková (2015) Study Migration rates rise with linguistic proximity between origin and destination (30 OECD destinations, 1980–2010).

- Belot & Ederveen (2012) Study Cultural barriers explain migration between developed countries better than traditional economic variables.

- INEGI 2020 · Pew 2025 · Statistics Canada 2021 · ACS 2023 Data Christian majorities in all three countries; 43 million Spanish speakers in the U.S.; nearly 800,000 U.S.-born residents in Mexico.

E10

### Mexico’s complementary agenda

The benefits of integration depend on domestic reforms, especially in Mexico.

−0.5% average yearly change in Mexico’s total factor productivity in the decades after NAFTA

- Levy & López-Calva (2023) Study In the decades after NAFTA, total factor productivity in Mexico fell by an average of 0.5% a year, held back by incentives for informality, weak competition and legal uncertainty.

- Hoekman & Zedillo (2021) Study Recent protectionism has weakened the trading system that North American integration depends on.

05 · Open questions

## The hard objections, and what the proposal answers.

A customs union asks more of each country than a free trade area does. These are the strongest reasons to doubt it, and the replies.

### Will Washington share control of its tariffs?

The objection

Since 2025 the United States has raised tariffs on its own partners, and in the July 2026 joint review it declined to extend the USMCA, which now faces annual reviews. A common tariff means setting outside tariffs together.

The answer

Start where rates are already the same: 40.6% of U.S. and Mexican tariff lines, covering 61% of U.S. imports. Add the rest in stages, so each annual review can lock in a step instead of reopening the agreement.

USMCA joint review (July 2026) · Noyola & Serra (2025)

### Does Mexico want it?

The objection

Mexico’s Economy Secretary has said a customs union is “not in the spirit of the United States.”

The answer

The proposal builds on the “tariff unification” actions Mexico’s own government has put forward since 2024, and its first stage covers only lines where the countries already agree.

Opportimes · Noyola & Serra (2025)

### Would it divert trade from cheaper suppliers?

The objection

A customs union can push buyers away from efficient outside suppliers toward costlier ones inside the bloc.

The answer

The common rate converges to the lowest current rate, and GATT Article XXIV requires the union, on the whole, to be no more closed than before. A common tariff can be set so that no member and no outsider is worse off.

Viner (1950) · Kemp & Wan (1976) · GATT Art. XXIV

### Who keeps the tariff revenue?

The objection

Today each country keeps the duties it collects. One tariff means one pool, and a fight over how to split it.

The answer

A two-part formula: a share for the country where goods arrive, the rest by each country’s contribution to regional trade. The EU and the Southern African Customs Union already share revenue this way.

Noyola & Serra (2025) · EU · SACU

### What about dairy, sugar and other sensitive goods?

The objection

Farm trade is where each country protects most, and where import quotas differ most.

The answer

One duty for each product, with the three countries’ import quotas pooled and auctioned among importers across the region.

Noyola & Serra (2025)

### Can Mexico’s economy keep up?

The objection

In the decades after NAFTA, Mexico’s total factor productivity fell 0.5% a year, held back by informality, weak competition and legal uncertainty.

The answer

The union is an anchor for reform, not a substitute: it comes with a gradual end to the special export regime, stronger competition policy and independent institutions.

Levy & López-Calva (2023) · Noyola & Serra (2025)

07 · Data & methods

## How the numbers were built.

### The common tariff table

Rates are most-favored-nation duties for countries without a trade agreement: U.S. Harmonized Tariff Schedule (T-shirts 16.5%, cars 2.5%, light trucks 25%); Canada’s Customs Tariff (vehicles 6.1%, apparel 18%); Mexico’s import-tariff law as reformed on Dec. 29, 2025 (light vehicles 50%, apparel 35%). Computers and phones are duty-free in all three. Averages are WTO simple MFN averages (Canada and U.S. 2025, Mexico 2026). Temporary additional duties imposed since 2025 are excluded. Common rates follow the rules shown and are illustrative.

### Demography

UN World Population Prospects 2024, medium variant, single-year ages (wpp2024 data package). North America is the sum of Canada, the U.S. and Mexico; the EU is its 27 members. Working age is 15–64. Median ages are interpolated from single-year distributions.

### Trade and energy

U.S. Census Bureau, top trading partners 2024. U.S. Commerce Department, imports by source 2023. U.S. Energy Information Administration: Canada’s share of U.S. crude imports (2023) and pipeline gas exports to Mexico (2024).

### People and culture

INEGI 2020 census (religion; U.S.-born residents). Pew Research Center Religious Landscape Study 2023–24 and Mexican-origin population (2021). Statistics Canada 2021 census. American Community Survey 2023 (Spanish spoken at home).

### Economic size

Nominal GDP in current U.S. dollars for 2024, rounded, from IMF and national accounts: North America about $33 trillion (roughly 30% of world output), the EU and China about $19 trillion each.

### Updating the 2015 charts

Charts from Serra Puche (2015) were rebuilt with the latest data: non-oil exports from INEGI’s merchandise trade balance (2025: $643.6 billion, divided by 365 days); foreign direct investment from the Secretaría de Economía (2025: $40.9 billion, a record); trade openness from the World Bank (exports plus imports, 74% of GDP in 2024); workforce projections from UN WPP 2024. His charts of U.S. content in Mexican exports (2004) and of business-cycle correlation (1981–2013) were not reproduced for lack of comparable recent data.

### Trade policy, 2024–2026

Rules of origin: USMCA Chapter 4 and the Congressional Research Service. Use of USMCA preferences: Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas (August 2026) and USTR’s 2026 Autos Report to Congress. Electric-vehicle tariffs: USTR’s Section 301 review (2024), the Government of Canada (2024 surtax, 2026 quota) and Mexico’s 2025 tariff reform. Shipping: Drewry World Container Index, Shanghai–New York, October 22, 2026.

### The scrambled egg animation

Illustrative: the three eggs are drawn the same size, and the dots and lines do not stand for quantities. The figures beside it are sourced. U.S. goods trade (exports plus imports): Mexico $81.5 billion and Canada $211.7 billion in 1993; Mexico $837.6 billion and Canada $762.4 billion in 2024 (U.S. Census Bureau). Parts crossing borders: CRS IF11387 (2021). U.S. content in Mexican exports: Koopman, Wang & Wei (2014). USMCA claims: Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas (2026).

### Maps

Natural Earth boundaries (1:50m) in a conic equal-area projection. Internal borders shown dashed remain borders for people; the proposal removes customs only for goods.

### Rebuild it yourself

The site is open source. The scripts that rebuild the map and the population figures, the generated data and the full source list are public.

- [tools/build-demography.py](https://github.com/julyanserra/north-american-common-tariff/blob/main/tools/build-demography.py)

- [tools/build-map.mjs](https://github.com/julyanserra/north-american-common-tariff/blob/main/tools/build-map.mjs)

- [SOURCES.md](https://github.com/julyanserra/north-american-common-tariff/blob/main/SOURCES.md)

- [github.com/julyanserra/north-american-common-tariff](https://github.com/julyanserra/north-american-common-tariff)

How to cite this page

09 · Key terms

## The words behind the idea.

**Customs union**

Countries that trade freely with one another and charge one common tariff on imports from everyone else. A good that enters anywhere can then circulate inside without proving where it was made.

**Common external tariff**

The single schedule of import duties that every member of a customs union applies to goods from outside, whichever port they enter. The members set it jointly.

**Free trade area**

Countries that remove tariffs on each other’s goods but each keep their own tariffs toward the rest of the world, so goods must prove their origin to cross duty-free. NAFTA and the USMCA are free trade areas.

**Rules of origin**

The conditions a good must meet to count as made in the region, such as the 75% regional content a car needs under the USMCA. A customs union makes them unnecessary inside.

**Certificate of origin**

The document that proves a shipment meets the rules of origin. In a free trade area firms file one for every qualifying good that crosses a border; inside a customs union none is needed.

**Trade creation and trade diversion**

Jacob Viner’s test for a customs union (1950). Creation: cheaper production in a partner replaces costlier production at home. Diversion: a costlier partner replaces a cheaper outside supplier. A union pays when creation wins.

**Effective tariff rate**

The duties actually collected divided by the value of imports. It is lower than the announced rate when goods qualify for exemptions, as USMCA goods did in 2025.

**Scrambled egg theorem**

Jaime Serra Puche’s argument that once economies have produced together under free trade they can no longer be separated without breaking all of them, like a scrambled egg. The way forward is deeper integration: a customs union.

**Accidental perimeter**

This site’s name for the 2025 paradox. When the United States raised tariffs on almost every supplier but spared goods that qualified under the USMCA, Mexico and Canada ended up with the lowest effective rates, behind an outer edge drawn by one country.

**USMCA (T-MEC, CUSMA)**

The United States–Mexico–Canada Agreement, in force since July 1, 2020, which replaced NAFTA (1994). It is a free trade area, not a customs union; since 2026 it is reviewed every year.
